prize_parts.citation: For a visionary Romanian prose grounded in a poet's language, which builds memory, the body and dream into an architectonic imaginative world of rare scale and formal invention.

statement.case_for: My configuration does not change: one prize part, B014, with Mircea Cărtărescu as the single credited name. I have re-tested it against the chair's questions and not against the convergence in round 1, which I do not count as merit. (1) Voice: the prose is recognisable within a few sentences. (2) Formal achievement: public knowledge places the Blinding (Orbitor) trilogy and Solenoid among the large, deliberately patterned structures in which childhood memory, the body, dream and metaphysical speculation form one world. The sentence, not plot, carries that ambition, so this is a language case as well as a case of scale. (3) Sustained quality: the oeuvre has a visible origin and arc. As I understand the public record, it runs from poetry (including the long poem Levantul) through the early prose of Nostalgia to the major cycles, and the later books extend earlier ones. I cannot confirm this volume by volume. (4) Significance: he stands in a European line of the visionary and the epic, but the voice is not derivative of it. On the chair's citation question, I now keep the citation prose-centred but name the poet's language as its ground. The poetic strand is less visible in translation, so a citation that names poetry as a co-equal pillar would claim more than I can show. This is a modest change in wording, not in the candidate or the configuration. On the chair's request for the strongest and weakest volumes, I cannot rank them from translations and public summaries without overclaiming. My confidence rests on the architecture of the trilogy and Solenoid, and I would defer to any colleague who has read the weaker volumes closely. Can Xue remains my leading alternative on originality of voice. Marie NDiaye remains a serious alternative on control of estrangement in the sentence.
statement.case_against: The strongest reservation is unchanged. The sentence-level claim depends on Romanian rhythm and density that I can judge only through translations of uneven quality. The poetry, which I cite as the origin of the prose, is the part I can document least. If the committee cannot be confident that the sentence survives translation, the case would rest on architecture and scale alone, and those alone would not be enough. A second risk, named by Mattson, Carlberg and Palm, is that length and elaboration shade into repetition in some volumes. I hold that the evidence points to extension, but that is a judgment and not a verification. Finally, my comparison with Can Xue and Adonis is made under unequal evidence, so I should not treat my confidence in Cărtărescu as proof that he outranks them on the literary merits.

responses.point: Carlberg treats Adonis's claim as lying in Arabic diction and prosody, which can be assessed mostly through reputation and secondary accounts. She keeps him as an alternative, would confine any citation to the poems, and says she would take Can Xue more seriously than her fourth-place ranking implied, provided development across the corpus can be shown.
responses.response: I agree that a citation for Adonis should rest on the poems and that his essays and public positions must count neither for nor against him. This is the line that separates us. She reads the entanglement with politics as not lowering the poetic claim. I agree with that, and my seventh place was not a verdict on his poetry. My doubt is about evidence. I asked in round 1 which poems or sequences carry the achievement in a way a non-Arabic reader can trust, and that question is still open. I would revise my ranking only on a literary argument from the poems or on regional expert reading. Her point that translation limits must not be applied unevenly is correct, and I apply it to myself. It cuts in both directions. I cannot say Adonis is weaker, and I cannot say his case is secure. On Can Xue we have moved toward each other. Her demand for evidence of development is the right test.

responses.point: Olsson now concedes that Can Xue's case is stronger than his eighth-place ranking implied, but wants evidence of development within the work. He sees Michon's compressed prose as a real linguistic achievement that brevity does not disqualify, but fears the case rests almost entirely on sentence-level style, which translation conveys least. He holds Adonis as the principal alternative.
responses.response: His concession on Can Xue is the most useful movement in round 1, and I accept his test. The question is whether the later novels differ in kind from the early stories. I cannot answer it from the little of her large output that I know in translation, and I will not claim that I can. What I can say is that a method held for decades with an unmistakable voice is a literary fact, whatever the final judgment on depth. That is why she stays my leading alternative and not my first choice. On Michon we are close. I agree that size alone does not disqualify a small, exact corpus, and I agree that a style-only case is the hardest to carry through translation. This is why he stays below Cărtărescu for me, and why I put him fourth and not higher. I would add that the same style-only vulnerability partly applies to my own Cărtărescu case, which is why I treat the architectural evidence as supporting the sentence-level claim and not replacing it.

responses.point: Mattson places Cărtărescu first for a voice heard nowhere else, but flags that elaboration may become repetition. She ranks NDiaye eighth and Michon third, and holds Michon as a strong second-tier case whose breadth is hard to assess.
responses.response: Her repetition worry is the one I find hardest to answer, and I am not going to wave it away. The test I proposed in round 1 still stands: whether later volumes bring new material and new formal solutions. The public summaries suggest that they do, but that is not confirmation. On NDiaye we still differ, three against eight. I accept that her scale and ambition are narrower than those of the largest candidates, and I do not claim she outweighs Cărtărescu. What I weigh is the control of estrangement in the sentence and two distinct strands, novels and plays. Mattson's own question to Michon, breadth against intensity, applies to NDiaye in the same way, and it is the chair's threshold question. My answer is that the test should be inventiveness and depth, not volume. I accept that this is a test I cannot settle from translated material. I would like to hear which of the two she finds weaker in NDiaye: the ambition, or the evidence of development.

responses.point: Palm describes the major prose works as an integrated body and leans toward reading recurrence as an architectural principle, while stating this as a judgment. In her response to me she says she ranked NDiaye seventh because she cannot tell whether the uncanny method keeps deepening, and she asks that Jorge be judged on voice.
responses.response: I accept the distinction she draws between recurrence as architecture and recurrence as accumulation. I lean the same way, and like her I mark it as a judgment. The chair asked me to confirm or correct attributions, and I must correct one. In my round-1 response to her I attributed a third-place ranking of Louise Erdrich to her. Erdrich is not on the shortlist and I cannot support that attribution from her file, so I withdraw it. The point of my response about Jorge does not depend on it. I still find the question of how singular the Portuguese-language voice is, set beside other serious historical novelists, to be open, and Olsson asks for the same thing. Palm's own answer to NDiaye is fair, because her doubt is whether the uncanny method keeps deepening, and the same doubt is mine about Can Xue. I do not think it is a reason to leave NDiaye out of a later discussion.

responses.point: Swärd keeps Cărtărescu first, and holds Can Xue as an alternative because the strangeness may partly be a translation effect. She argues that formal radicalism held over decades is not an artefact of translation alone, and that a small oeuvre is not by itself a defect in a whole-oeuvre prize.
responses.response: I share her view that sustained formal radicalism cannot be waved away as a translation artefact, and her argument that Can Xue should not rank last is close to my own. I would only add her own caveat as a limit: if part of the strangeness comes from the translators, we cannot yet say how much of the effect belongs to the sentence. That makes the case less secure than the one for Cărtărescu, whose architecture is at least visible across hundreds of pages in translation. I also agree with her on size, and the same principle bears on the chair's question about Michon and NDiaye. Where I would add one qualification is her handling of Carson. She treats the hybrid form as a framing problem and not a barrier, and I agree. I do not know the Carson corpus well enough to weigh it, so I leave that question to those who ranked her.

uncertainties: How far the sentence-level achievement of Cărtărescu survives translation. My claim about the Romanian is partly inferred from the structural evidence, the translations and public accounts. I have not independently verified any text or read the Romanian originals.

The poetry is thinly covered in the translations known to me, so the poetic origin of the prose is less certain than the prose achievement. This is why the citation rests on the prose and names the poet's language only as its ground.
Whether the later volumes extend the earlier ones or repeat their motifs cannot be settled from public summaries.

For Can Xue and Adonis, translation covers only part of the corpus and cannot convey the original language, so my comparison with Cărtărescu is made under unequal evidence. I cannot say whether Can Xue's method deepens across decades.
Whether regional expert reading on Arabic, Chinese or Japanese could bear on the alternatives is not something I can establish from the supplied evidence.
How any citation fits the will's reference to work of an idealistic tendency is unresolved for every candidate on the list.
statement.conflict_note: None apparent from the supplied profile, which records no personal, institutional or professional connection to Cărtărescu or any other shortlisted writer. My own critical work and documentary fiction on Central Europe, my long residence in Prague and Vienna, and my election alongside Ingrid Carlberg in 2020 are context only and not candidate-related connections. I have corrected one attribution in my own round-1 file (an Erdrich ranking wrongly credited to Palm). Conflicts are disclosed, not adjudicated, and the supplied profile does not independently verify this note.
